title_tamil: அகர முதல எழுத்தெல்லாம் ஆதி பகவன் முதற்றே உலகு
title_transliterated: Akara mudala ezhuththellaam aadhi bhagavan mudhatre ulagu
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: The first of 1330 couplets in the Thirukkural. Declares that as the letter 'A' is the origin of all letters, so is God (Aadhi Bhagavan) the origin of all creation. Universally celebrated as the most profound opening verse in Tamil literature.

title_tamil: கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் வாலறிவன் நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்
title_transliterated: Katradhanaal aaya payanen kol vaalariivan natral thozhaar enin
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: The second kural asks: what benefit has one gained from all that is learned, if one does not bow at the feet of He who is pure knowledge? Emphasizes devotion and learning as complementary virtues.

title_tamil: மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் மாணடி சேர்ந்தார் நிலர்மிசை நீடுவாழ் வார்
title_transliterated: Malarmisai eginaan maanadi serndhar nilarmisai needuvaazh vaar
title_english: Kural 3 - The Excellence of the Ascetic
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: Those who take refuge at the glorious feet of Him who walks on the lotus flower (Vishnu) shall live long and prosper on this earth. Celebrates devotion as the path to a long and prosperous life.

title_tamil: வேண்டுதல் வேண்டாமை இலானடி சேர்ந்தார்க்கு யாண்டும் இடும்பை இல
title_transliterated: Vendudhal vendaamai ilaanadi serndharku yaandum idumbai ila
title_english: Kural 4 - Assertion of the Strength of Virtue
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: Those who have reached the feet of Him who is free from both desire and aversion shall never suffer misfortune in any world. Describes the ultimate liberation attained through devotion to a desireless God.

title_tamil: இருள்சேர் இரண்டிலா வகன்மார்க்கம் காட்டும் அருள்சேர் அறிவினார் நட்பு
title_transliterated: Irulseer irandilaavagan maargam kaattum arulseer arivinaar natpu
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: The friendship of the wise who are filled with grace shows the path that is free from the two-fold darkness of ignorance and sin. Extols the value of association with the wise and compassionate.

title_tamil: பொறிவாயில் ஐந்தவித்தான் பொய்தீர் ஒழுக்க நெறிநின்றார் நீடுவாழ் வார்
title_transliterated: Porivaayil ainthaviththaan poidheer ozhukka nerinindraar needuvaazh vaar
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: Those who have controlled and suppressed the activity of the five senses and follow the true path of virtue shall live long. Celebrates the mastery of the senses as foundational to a virtuous long life.

title_tamil: தனக்குவமை இல்லாதான் தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் மனக்கவலை மாற்றல் அரிது
title_transliterated: Thanakkuvamai illaathaan thaalserndharku allaal manakkavalai maatral aridhu
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: Except for those who take refuge at the feet of Him who is without equal, it is difficult to remove the anxiety of the mind. States that mental peace belongs only to those devoted to the incomparable God.

title_tamil: அறவாழி அந்தணன் தாள்சேர்ந்தார்க் கல்லால் பிறவாழி நீந்தல் அரிது
title_transliterated: Aravaazhi andhannan thalserndharku allaal piravaazhi needhal aridhu
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: Except for those who take refuge at the feet of Him whose wheel is virtue, it is difficult to cross the ocean of birth. Uses the metaphor of the ocean of rebirth (samsara) to illustrate that only devotion grants liberation.

title_tamil: கோளில் பொறியின் குணமிலவே எண்குணத்தான் தாளை வணங்காத் தலை
title_transliterated: Kolil poriyil kunamilave en gunatthaan thaalai vanangathal thalai
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: A head that does not bow before the feet of Him who has eight virtues is as useless as a sense organ that cannot perform its function. Contrasts the worship of God with the futility of an organ that doesn't serve its purpose.

title_tamil: பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர் நீந்தார் இறைவன் அடிசேரா தார்
title_transliterated: Piravi perungadal needhuvar needhaar iraivan adisera dhaar
author: Thiruvalluvar
description: Those who clasp the feet of God shall swim across the great ocean of birth; those who do not shall not. Closes the first chapter with the definitive statement that divine devotion is the only means of crossing the cycle of rebirth.

title_english: Purananuru 192 - All Towns Are My Town
author: Kaniyan Pungundranar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: The most celebrated cosmopolitan verse of ancient Tamil literature. 'Every town is my hometown, every person is my kin.' Declares universal brotherhood transcending all geographical and social boundaries. Considered one of the earliest expressions of global humanism.

author: Pisiranthaiyar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A poem from the Purananuru extolling the valor and hospitality of warriors. Describes how even a seemingly small person can ignite great events, using the metaphor of fire starting from a spark. Reflects the heroic ethos of the Sangam age.

author: Maruthan Ilanagan
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: An akam (interior/love) poem exploring the longing of separation between lovers. Uses the imagery of the marutham landscape (agricultural riverine tracts) associated with infidelity and reconciliation. Exemplifies the akam genre's use of nature as an emotional mirror.

title_english: Kurunthokai 40 - What My Mother Was to Me
author: Sembulapeyanirar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: One of the most famous love poems in world literature. A woman speaks of her lover: 'What could my mother be to yours? What kin is my father to yours? And how did you and I meet? Yet our hearts are as red earth and pouring rain: mingled beyond parting.' Celebrated globally for its metaphor of inseparable union.

author: Kapilar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A kurinji (mountain landscape) poem by Kapilar, the most prolific of Sangam poets. Uses blooming mullai jasmine and forest imagery to express the joy and longing of a young woman waiting for her mountain-dwelling lover. Kapilar is credited with over 200 poems across multiple anthologies.

author: Nallantuvanar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A poem from the Kalittokai, composed in the kali meter associated with drama and debate. Uses the paalai (desert) landscape to depict the anguish of separation. The Kalittokai is unique among Sangam anthologies for its dramatic dialogues and near-theatrical presentation of love's stages.

author: Palaipaddiya Perungatunko
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A Natrinai poem using the moonlit mountain peak as an extended metaphor for the luminous presence of the beloved. Exemplifies the sangam convention of tinai (landscape-emotion correspondence) where the kurinji mountain terrain signals pre-marital union and longing.

author: Avvaiyar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A poem by the celebrated poet Avvaiyar, one of the few prominent female voices in Sangam literature. Meditates on the true nature of wealth as something to be shared and given, not hoarded. Avvaiyar is also known for her didactic works Aathichudi and Konraivendan.

author: Nalveliyar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A neithal (coastal) landscape poem from Akananuru depicting water lilies blooming by the shore as a metaphor for longing and patient waiting. The coastal tinai in Sangam poetics is associated with the theme of pining for an absent lover who has gone to sea.

author: Ponmudiyar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: An elegy on the heroic death of a warrior, drawing from the puram tradition of exterior poetry about war, death, and honor. Illustrates the Sangam-age Tamil warrior code where dying in battle was considered the highest honor, and mothers celebrated the bravery of their fallen sons.

author: Ilango Adigal
description: The opening of the Puhar Canto of Silappathikaram, one of the five great Tamil epics. Set in the Chola port city of Kaveri Poompattinnam (Puhar/Kaveripoompattinam). Introduces Kovalan and Kannagi and their life in the prosperous city. Ilango Adigal was a Jain monk and prince who renounced his throne to compose this masterwork.

author: Ilango Adigal
description: The tragic climax of the Silappathikaram set in the Pandya capital Madurai. Kovalan is unjustly executed by the Pandya king's soldiers who mistake his anklet for one stolen from the queen. Kannagi's devastating grief and righteous fury leads to the destruction of Madurai—a supreme statement on justice and wifely devotion.

author: Ilango Adigal
description: Kannagi tears off her left breast and hurls it at the city of Madurai in grief and fury, causing it to burn. She confronts the Pandya king who dies of shame and the queen follows. Kannagi's figure has become the eternal symbol of Tamil womanhood, justice, and the power of chastity (karpu). Her statue stands in Chennai today.

author: Ilango Adigal
chapter: Vanji Canto - Kuravai Dance on the Hills
description: The Vanji Canto set in the Chera kingdom, where Kannagi is deified. Features the Kuravai (hill dance) performed in her honor. Contains remarkable musical notation passages describing the classical Tamil music system with 72 melakarta ragas referenced centuries before modern carnatic codification.

author: Ilango Adigal
description: Describes the grand Indra Festival in the Chola port city of Puhar, providing an invaluable historical record of ancient Tamil urban life, trade, arts, and religious festivals. An extraordinary source for historians on ancient Tamil urban civilization and the multicultural commerce of the ancient world.

author: Sithalai Chathanar
description: The sequel to Silappathikaram, following Manimekalai, the daughter of Kovalan and the courtesan Madhavi. Abandoning a life of dance and beauty, she becomes a Buddhist nun. A deeply philosophical Buddhist epic that debates the nature of reality, the existence of a soul, and the path to liberation. Unique in Tamil literature for its detailed exposition of Buddhist logic and philosophy.

title_english: Manimekalai - The Teachings of the Tripitaka
author: Sithalai Chathanar
description: A philosophical cantos from Manimekalai containing discourses on Buddhist teachings. The epic systematically presents the arguments of various philosophical schools including Sankhya, Vaisheshika, Ajivika, and Charvaka before demonstrating the superiority of Buddhist logic. An unparalleled document for the history of Indian philosophy.

author: Sithalai Chathanar
description: Manimekalai receives the Amudhasurabi, a divine inexhaustible vessel that can feed the hungry endlessly. She uses it to feed the poor and oppressed. This episode articulates a Buddhist social ethics of compassion and the obligation to eliminate hunger—remarkably ahead of its time in envisioning a welfare state.

author: Kambar
description: The opening canto of Kambar's Tamil rendering of the Ramayana, considered one of the greatest literary achievements in any language. Kambar's Ramayana is not a mere translation but an independent creative work. The Bala Kanda establishes the cosmological and geographical setting with stunning poetic imagery.

author: Kambar
description: The Sundara Kanda of Kambar's epic, describing Hanuman's leap to Lanka and his meeting with Sita. Kambar's poetic innovations in describing the ocean crossing and the city of Lanka are considered unparalleled. His characterization deepens all Valmiki's characters with psychological and devotional dimensions unique to Tamil Shaiva and Vaishnava traditions.

author: Kambar
description: The war canto of Kambaramayanam depicting the great battle between Rama's army and Ravana's forces. Kambar's battle poetry is considered supreme in Tamil literature for its energy, imagery, and dramatic tension. The death of Ravana is rendered with unexpected pathos, presenting him as a tragic hero who fell through pride.

author: Kambar
description: The forest canto describing Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana's years in the Dandaka forest and the abduction of Sita by Ravana. Kambar introduces extensive nature poetry in the Tamil akam tradition, transforming the forest episodes into a profound meditation on beauty, loss, and dharma rooted in Tamil literary sensibility.

title_english: Kambaramayanam - The Kingdom of the Monkeys
author: Kambar
chapter: Kishkindha Kanda - Alliance with the Monkeys
description: Describes Rama's alliance with Sugriva and the monkey kingdom of Kishkindha. Kambar's depiction of Hanuman here becomes a theological statement on bhakti—total devotion as the highest path. The meeting of Rama and Hanuman is rendered as the union of god and his greatest devotee, shaping Tamil Vaishnavism profoundly.

title_english: Tevaram - Appar: Lord of the Golden Form
author: Appar
description: A devotional hymn by Appar (Thirunavukkarasar), one of the four principal Nayanmars (Shaivite saints). Appar was a former Jain who converted to Shaivism and composed 4900 hymns. This hymn praises Shiva as the lord with a form of gold, and is sung in Shaiva temples across Tamil Nadu. The Tevaram became the Dravidian Veda.

title_english: Tevaram - Appar: Save Me from Yama
author: Appar
chapter: Appar's Hymns - On liberation from death
description: A powerful plea to Shiva to repel Yama (god of death) and grant liberation. Appar composed this while enduring persecution. Known for its deeply personal, emotionally raw devotion. Appar's biography—his conversion, imprisonment by the Pallava king, and miraculous release through Shiva's grace—is itself a legend in Tamil Shaivism.

title_english: Tevaram - Sambandar: Shiva Who Wears the Ear Ring
author: Thirugnana Sambandar
description: The very first hymn in the Tevaram collection by Sambandar, sung as an infant at age three. Describes the cosmic form of Shiva with his earring, crescent moon, and bull. Sambandar is said to have sung 4158 hymns. This opening hymn is the most commonly sung in Shaiva temple worship across the Tamil world, chanted daily for over 1300 years.

title_english: Tevaram - Sambandar: Lord of the Broad Pearl-Garland Chest
author: Thirugnana Sambandar
description: A Tevaram hymn by Sambandar praising Shiva as the lord adorned with a garland of pearls. Sambandar is credited with reversing the spread of Jainism in South India and converting the Pandya king back to Shaivism. His hymns exhibit extraordinary musical sophistication—each set in a specific raga and tala.

title_english: Tevaram - Sundarar: O Beloved Madman with the Crescent Moon
author: Sundarar
description: The opening hymn of Sundarar, addressed to Shiva in a tone of extraordinary intimacy and even loving reproach—calling God 'madman' (piththaa). Sundarar, who called himself Thondaradipodi (dust of devotees' feet), had a famously personal, friend-like relationship with Shiva. This hymn established a new devotional mode in Shaivism: the friend-devotee.

title_english: Tevaram - Sundarar: The Anthology of Holy Servants
author: Sundarar
description: Sundarar's famous hymn listing all 63 Nayanmar (Shaivite) saints. This short hymn became the seed text for the Periya Puranam, the great hagiographic epic of the Tamil Shaiva saints by Sekkizhar. It is the primary source for the names and tradition of the 63 nayanmars and is sung as a liturgical prayer in all Shaiva temples.

author: Andal
description: The opening pasuram of Thiruppavai, Andal's 30-verse devotional poem. Describes the month of Margazhi and the vow (pavai nonbu) taken by the gopika girls (cowherd girls) to worship Vishnu. Andal is the only female Alvar saint, and her Thiruppavai is recited daily during the Margazhi month in all Vaishnava temples. She longed to marry Vishnu himself and is considered his consort.

title_english: Thiruppavai 2 - O Beings Who Live on Earth
author: Andal
description: The second pasuram calls all beings of the world to participate in the vow. Andal lists the disciplines: no eating of butter, no applying of eye-liner until the vow is fulfilled and Vishnu is pleased. This verse establishes the communal and democratic nature of bhakti—available to all, regardless of caste or status.

title_english: Thiruppavai 3 - The Excellent One Who Measured the Universe
author: Andal
description: Praises Vishnu as Vamana who grew to measure all three worlds in two strides. Andal describes the cosmic god as approachable through simple devotion—rain will fall, harvests will be plentiful, and all disease will end if he is pleased. Connects cosmic divine power to earthly abundance, linking theology to ecology.

author: Anonymous (Jain Monks compilation)
description: A verse from Naladiyar listing jealousy, greed, anger, and harsh speech as the four vices that destroy a person. The Naladiyar is a collection of 400 four-line poems compiled by Jain monks. Along with the Thirukkural, it represents the pinnacle of classical Tamil didactic (neethi) literature. The work was reportedly composed by 400 different poets.

title_english: Naladiyar - Those Who Mortify the Body
author: Anonymous (Jain Monks compilation)
description: A verse on the value of asceticism and compassion for all living beings. Those who torment the body but have no compassion for the soul gain nothing. Reflects the Jain ahimsa (non-violence) philosophy that permeates the Naladiyar. The text shows the deep intermingling of Tamil and Jain ethics.

title_english: Naladiyar - On the Company One Keeps
author: Anonymous (Jain Monks compilation)
description: A quatrain on how a person's character is shaped by the company they keep—associating with the ignoble degrades even the virtuous, while the company of the great elevates even the small. One of many Naladiyar verses on the critical importance of sangam (good company), a theme shared with the Thirukkural.

title_english: Naladiyar - The Word of a Chaste Woman
author: Anonymous (Jain Monks compilation)
description: A verse on the power and weight of the word of a woman of virtue (karpu). Her blessings and curses carry immense power. This verse reflects the broader Tamil literary tradition of highly honoring female virtue and the supernatural power attributed to it, a theme central to Silappathikaram's narrative.

author: Manickavasagar
description: The opening masterwork of the Thiruvasagam. 'Namasivaya vaazha' — it begins with the panchakshara mantra and proceeds through a cosmic vision of Shiva as the omnipresent reality. G.U. Pope, who translated the Thiruvasagam into English in 1900, declared that he who has read the Thiruvasagam cannot but love Manickavasagar. Called the most heart-melting devotional poetry in Tamil.

title_english: Thiruvasagam - Hymn of the Ancient Temple
author: Manickavasagar
description: Manickavasagar's hymn on the sacred temple of Chidambaram, dwelling place of Nataraja—Shiva as the cosmic dancer. Manickavasagar was a minister who gave away the king's treasury to build this temple. His hymns describe Shiva's grace in intensely personal terms of surrender and transformation, establishing the Chidambaram temple's theological supremacy.

author: Manickavasagar
description: The Thiruvembavai, Manickavasagar's Shaiva parallel to Andal's Thiruppavai. Twenty hymns describing girls who wake before dawn in the Margazhi month to bathe in cold water and worship Shiva. Sung daily during Margazhi in Shaiva temples. The structural parallel between Thiruppavai and Thiruvembavai reflects the rich interfaith devotional dialogue within Tamil literature.

title_english: Purananuru - Long Live the Face of the Earth
author: Mudathama Kanniyar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
chapter: Poem on the permanence of virtue
description: A Purananuru poem celebrating the earth and virtue as eternal. While kings come and go, the earth and righteous deeds endure. Part of the puram tradition of philosophical poetry that situates human drama within the larger frame of cosmic continuity. Exemplifies the Sangam worldview where nature is the eternal witness to human actions.

author: Murinjiyur Mudinagarayar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A Natrinai poem using the song of the cuckoo bird in summer as a metaphor for the anguish of a young woman separated from her mountain lover. The cuckoo's call, heard in the blooming mullai forest, intensifies her longing unbearably. Illustrates Sangam poetry's mastery of using specific seasonal flora and fauna as precise emotional signals.

author: Maruthan Ilanagan
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: A Marutham kali poem (associated with agricultural riverine tracts and the theme of infidelity and reconciliation). A woman confronts her unfaithful husband in a dramatic dialogue that reads like theatre. The Kalittokai's dramatic dialogues are unique in Sangam literature and have been called the earliest dramatic poetry in Tamil.

author: Kapilar
era: Sangam period, 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE
description: One of Kapilar's celebrated mountain (kurinji) poems from Akananuru. Uses the imagery of the mountain gooseberry, waterfalls, and elephant herds to evoke the secret union of young lovers in the mountains. Kapilar is credited with being a brahmin poet who celebrated Tamil culture and was a companion of the Chera king Cheran Chenkuttuvan.
